content: Tinea capitis, also referred to as Herpes tonsurans, Ringworm of the scalp, or Scalp ringworm, is a superficial fungal infection of the scalp caused by dermatophytes, primarily from the Trichophyton and Microsporum genera. These fungi invade the hair shaft, leading to clinical manifestations such as single or multiple patches of hair loss, often with a characteristic black dot appearance due to broken hairs. Other symptoms may include inflammation, scaling, pustules, and pruritus (itching). This condition predominantly affects pre-pubertal children, with boys being more commonly affected than girls. It is rare in adults. At least eight species of dermatophytes are implicated in tinea capitis, with Trichophyton species being more prevalent in regions such as Central America, the United States, and parts of Western Europe, while Microsporum species are more common in South America, Southern and Central Europe, Africa, and the Middle East. The infection is contagious and can spread through direct contact with infected individuals, animals, or contaminated objects. In some cases, the fungus may exist on the scalp without causing symptoms, a state known as asymptomatic carriage. Treatment requires oral antifungal agents, with griseofulvin being the most commonly prescribed medication. Newer antifungal agents, such as terbinafine, itraconazole, and fluconazole, are also gaining acceptance. The symptoms of tinea capitis can vary. It may present as thickened, scaly, and sometimes boggy swellings or as expanding, raised, red rings resembling classic ringworm. Common symptoms include severe scalp itching, dandruff, and bald patches where the fungus has invaded the skin. The condition can mimic other scalp disorders, such as seborrheic dermatitis or dandruff. There are three main types of tinea capitis, classified based on the causative organism and clinical presentation: microsporosis, trichophytosis, and favus. Microsporosis typically begins as a small red papule around a hair shaft, which later becomes scaly. The affected hairs break off 1–3 mm above the scalp. Historically, Microsporum audouinii was the primary causative agent, but in Europe, Microsporum canis is now more common. This species is often transmitted from sick cats and kittens, as well as through person-to-person contact or shared contaminated items like brushes and combs. Trichophytosis, caused by Trichophyton tonsurans in the United States and Trichophyton violaceum in regions like Eastern Europe, Africa, and India, presents as dry, non-inflammatory patches with angular shapes. When hairs break off at the follicle opening, black dots are left behind. Favus, caused by Trichophyton schoenleinii, is endemic in South Africa and the Middle East. It is characterized by yellowish, cup-shaped crusts (scutula) grouped in patches resembling a honeycomb. These lesions enlarge and become crusted, with the characteristic appearance visible only at the edges of the scabs. Diagnosing tinea capitis can be challenging, as it may resemble other conditions like psoriasis or seborrheic dermatitis. Diagnosis is confirmed through microscopic examination and fungal culture of epilated hairs. A Wood's lamp examination can reveal fluorescence in hairs infected by certain Microsporum species, such as M. canis, M. audouinii, M. rivalieri, and M. ferrugineum, which fluoresce bright green to yellow-green. In contrast, Trichophyton schoenleinii infections produce a dull green or blue-white fluorescence. Trichoscopy of M. canis infections may show characteristic comma hairs. Histopathological examination of scalp biopsies reveals sparse fungal elements in the stratum corneum and hyphae extending into the hair follicle, often accompanied by local inflammatory reactions. The treatment of choice for tinea capitis is oral griseofulvin, a fungistatic agent derived from Penicillium species. It disrupts fungal microtubules, interfering with mitosis and cytoplasmic microtubules. The recommended pediatric dosage is 10 mg/kg/day for 6–8 weeks, which may be increased to 20 mg/kg/day for infections caused by Trichophyton tonsurans or in cases of treatment failure. Unlike topical antifungal treatments, oral therapy is necessary to penetrate the hair shaft where the fungus resides. Griseofulvin has a high efficacy rate, ranging from 88% to 100%. Other oral antifungal agents, such as terbinafine, itraconazole, and fluconazole, offer shorter treatment durations but may carry risks of rare side effects, such as hepatotoxicity or drug interactions, and are generally more expensive. In 2007, the FDA approved terbinafine (Lamisil) for use in children aged four years and older. This medication is available in granule form, which can be sprinkled on food, but it carries a risk of liver toxicity and may cause a metallic taste. The pathophysiology of tinea capitis involves fungal invasion of the stratum corneum and subsequent penetration into keratinized structures. Dermatophytes produce keratinase, an enzyme that allows them to utilize keratin as a nutrient source. Infected hairs become brittle, and clinical signs of broken hairs typically appear after three weeks. There are three types of fungal invasion: Ectothrix: Fungal spores (arthroconidia) grow on the exterior of the hair shaft. Infected hairs fluoresce greenish-yellow under a Wood's lamp. This type is associated with Microsporum canis, Microsporum gypseum, Trichophyton equinum, and Trichophyton verrucosum. Endothrix: Arthroconidia are confined within the hair shaft, with the cuticle remaining intact. This type does not fluoresce under a Wood's lamp and is associated with anthropophilic species like Trichophyton tonsurans and Trichophyton violaceum. Favus: This type causes crusting on the skin surface and hair loss and is associated with Trichophyton schoenleinii. Epidemiologically, tinea capitis is a contagious disease endemic in many regions, primarily affecting pre-pubertal children aged 6 to 10 years. It is more common in males and rarely persists beyond adolescence. Transmission occurs through direct contact with infected individuals or indirectly via contaminated objects (fomites). In the United States, the prevalence is estimated at 3–8% of the pediatric population, with up to one-third of households with an infected individual harboring asymptomatic carriers. The causative fungal species vary by geographic region and have shifted over time. For example, Microsporum audouinii was once the predominant species in North America and Europe but has been largely replaced by Trichophyton tonsurans in the United States. This shift is attributed to the widespread use of griseofulvin, which is more effective against M. audouinii, as well as changes in immigration patterns and international travel. Trichophyton violaceum has also become more prevalent, particularly in urban populations in the United Kingdom and Europe.
